newsitem.title: Japan: North Korean leader's birthday marred by defection.
newsitem.headline: North Korean leader's birthday marred by defection.

text.p: North Korean leader Kim Jong-il celebrated his 55th birthday on Sunday, but the occasion was overshadowed by the surprise defection of his top adviser, talk of a power struggle and a worsening food crisis.
North Korea's state-run media heaped praise on Kim Jong-il and state television, received in Hong Kong, showed happy crowds attending firework celebrations, apparently on Saturday night.

Tokyo-based Radiopress news service, which closely monitors North Korean broadcasts, said earlier it detected no "festive mood" in Pyongyang with no major events planned except a gymnastics display by several thousand young people.
North Korea's state-run radio stations abruptly cancelled their scheduled live coverage of the event without explanation.
Korea watchers in Tokyo believe Kim was forced to scale down birthday functions mainly because of severe food shortages caused by two consecutive years of flooding.

"There has been some bad news for North Korea, such as the defection of a top official. But more than anything else, food shortages must be the biggest factor," Shinya Kato, an expert on North Korea at Radiopress, told Reuters.
Other analysts say the North Korean leadership could risk a backlash by staging lavish events for the birthday.
"It's dangerous to invite tens of thousands of hungry citizens to the North Korean capital," said Nozomu Akizuki, professor of Northeast Asian diplomacy at Tokai University.
"You have to remember that people down there are really starving. They could even challenge Kim Jong-il," he said.
The defection of top Pyongyang ideologue Hwang Jang-yop has only added to the reclusive Stalinist state's woes.
Hwang, 73, was a pillar of the North Korean establishment and a senior aide to Kim Jong-il.
He and an aide took a taxi to South Korea's consulate in Beijing on Wednesday and asked for asylum. Hwang remains trapped in the compound as negotiations continue to bring him to Seoul.

The defection -- Pyongyang has called it a kidnapping -- has dragged China into a heated row that has bred fears of renewed tension on the Korean peninsula and possibly a disastrous collapse of the communist North.
The climate worsened on Saturday when another North Korean defector was shot and seriously injured near Seoul and South Korea said it suspected North Korean agents.
A senior Japanese government official said Hwang's defection could set off a power struggle that would lead to more defections, a refugee flight and the ultimate collapse of the communist regime.
"Now everyone in North Korea's ruling structure is going to be suspicious of everyone else, as well as their own future, and that could prompt a really destructive power struggle," the official said.
Meanwhile, the North Korean media lavished praise on Kim Jong-il and tacitly denied that there was any power struggle in Pyongyang.

"Political stability (in North Korea) is founded upon the lofty power of our comrade Kim Jong-il whose leadership position is trusted and supported by our people," North Korea's official newspaper Rodong Sinmun said in Sunday's editorial.
Although North Korea's domestic media made no mention of Hwang's defection, a top North Korean official suggested that there were "separatists" in North Korea.

"He (Kim Jong-il) has guided all the patriotic forces at home and abroad..., containing the line of confrontation, war and division pursued by the domestic and foreign separatists with the line of independence, peaceful reunification and great national unity," Kim Ki-nam, a top ruling party official, told a Pyongyang meeting late on Saturday.

Kim Jong-il, supreme commander of the country's 1.1-million-strong military, has yet to be formally confirmed in two key posts held by his late father Kim Il-sung -- general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president.
